# What does this word mean?

Two pages using one word for different things cost a team an afternoon. This page fixes each word once, in plain language, and every other page defers to it.

Example: a plan schedules work in "waves" while the pipeline runs in "stages". They are different things. Wave and Flow stage below stay separate entries so the two never collide.

- **Mission**: one governed unit of work under `.mugiwara/missions/<name>/`, from triage to closure and archive.
- **Flow stage**: one pipeline step, Flow 0 (triage) through Flow 9 (closure). The user-facing word for a stage.
- **Wave**: an ordered group of tasks Zoro runs together. Nami's plan lists tasks in waves. A wave is never a stage and never a directory name.
- **flows/**: the mission directory holding one file per stage. Files are numbered in the order written, not by stage number. Older missions that kept a `waves/` directory stay on it.
- **Lane**: the process size for a change: direct, lean, standard, full or spike. Computed from the diff. Sensitive paths force full.
- **Mode**: how often the crew asks you: guided, semi or auto. Set in `.mugiwara/config`. A mission keeps the mode it started in.
- **Execution posture**: how work runs, for example inline one task after another, or in parallel workers. Chosen at stage boundaries and recorded in the decision trail. Independent of mode and cost.
- **Cost governor**: the part of the crew that watches process spend against the lane budget and records warn or stop decisions. It recommends and records. It never silently skips a safety stage.
- **Slop**: wasted work the governor flags: repeated reads, needless abstraction, a fix loop going nowhere, out-of-scope changes.
- **Savepoint**: the state snapshot written at each stage boundary. Resume and every computed command read it. Normally automatic.
- **Continue**: resume that prints the exact pickup point without running anything.
- **Evidence**: the recorded output behind a claim. A claim without evidence does not pass a stage.
- **Gate**: a pass or fail check with evidence. No negotiation.
- **Blocker ledger**: the list of failures that need help. Shipping needs it empty or every row owned.
- **Heal cycle**: one fix-and-recheck attempt by Brook. The limit is the `heal_max_cycles` config key (3 by default). After that the crew hands the failure to a human.
- **Banner**: the one heading line that marks the start of a stage. Its absence means the stage was skipped, and that is recorded.
- **Check-in**: Luffy's boundary report: what happened, evidence links, next step.
- **Trail**: everything under `.mugiwara/`: plans, stage files, findings, decisions, blockers. It folds into `report.md` at archive.
- **Archive**: folding the trail into `report.md` once the integrity checks pass.
- **Provenance**: a record of which mission, lane and evidence produced a change. See [signing and provenance](../optional/signing.md).
- **Policy**: `mugiwara.policy.yml`, org rules that push lanes and thresholds up only. See [policy](../concepts/policy.md).
- **Index budget**: the 5,500-character ceiling on skill and agent descriptions that load at the start of every session.

Counts everywhere: 14 skills, 11 agents (+2 internal).

# Harness Matrix

You switch editors and the crew behaves differently. Skills that auto-fired now sit idle, or agents that dispatched now narrate instead. This page answers "which harness supports what" with one example, then the tier table. Loading differs per tier. Workflow, lane sizing, and evidence discipline stay identical.

Example: on Claude Code a security audit on a sensitive path dispatches Jinbe as a subagent; on tier 3 the main thread plays Jinbe inline from `.mugiwara/refs/`.

Rule: every skill and agent file ships to every harness. The tier decides native trigger versus rules file versus stub pointer. A conformance script (`scripts/conformance.ts`) checks every installable target against golden files in CI.

| Tier | Harnesses | Loading | Scope | CLI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Claude Code, opencode, Codex, Cursor (first-class) | Native skills, native agent files | Global plus project | Bundled |
| 2 | Copilot (community, best effort) | Stub pointer, body in `.mugiwara/refs/` | Global plus project | npx only |
| 3 | Windsurf, Cline, Kilo, Antigravity, Gemini (community, best effort) | Stub pointer, body in `.mugiwara/refs/` | Project only | Shell fallback |
| Marketplace | Kimi, Pi (community, best effort) | Manifest plus content pointers | Per host | npx only |

**Host status (as of 2026-11-01).** "Smoke" is `bun run smoke` (`scripts/smoke-lifecycle.ts`): install, upgrade and uninstall in a temp repo, checking files only.

| Host | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | Tested end to end | Real host |
| opencode | Tested end to end | Real host |
| Codex | Install verified by smoke only | Files only. A 2026-10-19 real run was partial: review dispatch failed |
| Cursor | Install verified by smoke only | Not run in a real Cursor |
| Claude Code marketplace commands (`/plugin marketplace add`, `/plugin install`) | Unverified | Not exercised by smoke or a recorded run |
| Other community hosts | Not run in the real host | Conformance goldens only; Kimi and Pi are manifest only |

First-class means native files and a conformance golden (`test/golden/<id>.json`). Community targets are best effort.

**Codex and Cursor enforcement.** Both ship skills and agents natively and nothing else: no hooks, runtime write-scope or irreversible-command guard. Codex custom agents cannot override `sandbox_mode`; Cursor's `readonly` would block `.mugiwara/**` writes so it is unused. Independent review and agent dispatch are unverified on both. Keep the four-dispatch-worthy rule below and use inline review when dispatch is unavailable. The Codex plugin and Cursor plugin manifests ship skills only (agent bundling undocumented).

**"Dispatchable agents" is not one behavior.** opencode's agent switch is a
foreground, context-preserving mode change: the same session keeps
narrating, wearing a different persona. Claude Code's (and, natively,
Copilot's) agent dispatch is a background, zero-context subagent: a fresh
instance with no memory of the conversation that called it, its result
surfacing only after it finishes. Treating the two as interchangeable breaks
any persona whose job is continuous cross-flow-stage routing.

Only four personas are dispatch-worthy under the isolated model: bounded,
evidence-in/verdict-out roles that can reconstruct everything they need from
`.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/**`: `zoro-execution` (parallel workers),
`brook-healing` (heal workers), `robin-reviewer`, `jinbe-security` (parallel
review). The other nine personas, `luffy-orchestrator` above all since it
alone owns live routing and the decision log across the whole mission, must
run inline: embodied by the main thread via `/mugiwara` or the equivalent
natural-language trigger, never invoked directly through an isolated-dispatch
tool. `luffy-orchestrator.md` carries a self-check guard for this; see its
"Dispatch guard" section.

Copilot ships the identical crew files and is documented as having "native
worker dispatch" for auditor/reviewer roles (see [install](../install.md)), but
whether its dispatch mechanism isolates context the same way Claude Code's
does, and therefore whether `luffy-orchestrator` is exposed to the same
misuse there, is **unverified**. Treat Copilot as same-risk-until-tested,
not as confirmed-safe.

**Independent review.** With `independent_review=on`, Luffy dispatches `robin-reviewer` and `jinbe-security` as separate subagents on the full lane or a sensitive path. Claude Code supports this. Not verified: opencode (its agent switch keeps the conversation, so it may not give a fresh context), Copilot, Codex and Cursor (dispatch behavior untested). Those hosts, and every inline-only tier, have no ledger and no closure gate, and run the review inline and the report says `Checked inline`. The ledger that backs the label is written by a Claude Code hook, so no other host produces an independent label today (ASSUMPTION: no hook equivalent was run elsewhere).

Without the CLI there is no machine-readable state. Savepoint, archive, continue, and sign need it. The crew still runs the pipeline and still writes an inline report, but resume, budget tracking, lane memory, and the closure integrity gate stay inactive. The crew announces this at Flow 0.

Write scope is runtime-enforced on opencode for internal agents only. Claude Code blocks edits for artifact agents with partial cover. All other targets carry the constraint as prose plus validator gates. Worker dispatch is native on Claude Code, opencode, and Copilot; Codex and Cursor have native agent files but dispatch behavior is unverified. Elsewhere the fallback is savepoint plus checkpoint plus a fresh session through resume. The plan doc stays the source of truth on every host.

## Enforcement per target

Hooks are the only mechanism that produces a mission artifact without a model choosing to, and they are not portable.

- **Turn-end enforcement.** Claude Code: enforced, because `Stop` and `SubagentStop` run `hooks/auto-savepoint.ts`. opencode: a warning at session end, because the `session.idle` event surfaces work without triage. Every other target, including Codex and Cursor: advisory only, with no hook mechanism at all.
- **Irreversible-command guard.** Claude Code: enforced, because `PreToolUse` on Bash runs `hooks/pretool-guard.js`. opencode: enforced, because `tool.execute.before` on bash throws (same table as `src/guards.ts`, parity-tested). Every other target, including Codex and Cursor: prose only.

# Runbook: Monorepo with per-package lanes

One repo-wide lane sizes a one-package fix like a whole-repo migration. Scoping the lane to your package stops that.

**When to use this:** one repo holds several packages and the repo-wide lane oversizes small changes.
**Time:** about 10 minutes of setup, then the normal flow.
**You need:** the monorepo checkout and your package path.

## Steps

1. Scope lane sizing to one package in `.mugiwara/config`. The setting is read by the lane and savepoint scripts.
   ```ini
   lane_scope_glob=packages/api/**
   ```
2. Record a savepoint (the state snapshot the crew writes at each stage boundary, so this normally happens on its own). The lane now sizes from matching files only.
   ```bash
   mugiwara savepoint m "" 1 guided
   ```
   ```
   ✓ savepoint written: .mugiwara/missions/m/state.json (lane=direct, flow=1, files=1)
   ```
3. Give each package its own row in the plan's sub-missions table, so `mugiwara plan conflict-check plan.md` compares file sets per package.
4. Teammates in other packages repeat step 1 with their own glob (`packages/web/**`) on their branch before their first savepoint.
5. Close per package: `mugiwara archive <mission>` folds only that mission's files. A bare `archive` lists the missions to pick from (exit 2) instead of guessing.

Sensitive-path escalation still reads the whole diff, so scoping never hides an `auth/` change in another package.

## If something goes wrong

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| the lane looks too big for a tiny package change | the glob is unset, so the whole repo counts | set `lane_scope_glob` to the package path and run the savepoint again |
| the conflict check flags two packages | the plan rows share files | narrow each row's Touched Files to its package directory |
| `multiple missions on disk … specify <mission>` | the short form cannot infer the mission | `mugiwara savepoint --flow 2 <mission>` |

## What you end up with

Each package slice sizes, runs and archives on its own lane, while the repo root keeps one shared config and one archive index.

# Runbook: Resume after a crash, context loss or machine switch

The session died and the plan lives on disk, not in your context. Rebuild the picture from saved state instead of starting over.

**When to use this:** the session ended, the context filled up, you changed laptop, or you switched branch.
**Time:** about 2 minutes when state is intact.
**You need:** the repo checked out (the same branch if possible) and the crew installed.

Outputs are from a real v1.0.5 run.

## Steps

1. One mission, one handle: print the exact resume point.
   ```bash
   mugiwara continue crew1 jane-doe
   ```
   ```
   Resumed: crew1 [jane-doe], Flow 2, 0/0 tasks — next_action: verify this flow stage against the plan, then continue per plan (next stage or closure) — run: (no next_session_prompt recorded)
   ```
2. Several missions: list them, then pick one. The command exits with code 2 on purpose so a script never guesses for you.
   ```bash
   mugiwara continue
   ```
   ```
   3 missions in flight:

     MISSION  MEMBER           FLOW  TASKS  LANE    MODE
     crew1    jane-doe         2     0/0    direct  guided
     crew1    john-smith       2     0/0    direct  guided
     other    —                1     0/0    direct  guided

   Pick one: mugiwara continue <mission> [member]
   ```
3. Check `next_action` against `plan.md` before executing. The printed state is computed from files, not a judgment call.
4. Handing the work to someone else? Write the report they can act on.
   ```bash
   mugiwara handoff other
   ```
   ```
   # Handoff: other

   … [trimmed]
   | Mission | flow 1, tasks 0/0, lane direct, mode guided |
   | Branch | `main` |
   | Actor | <git author name> |
   … [trimmed]
   written: .mugiwara/missions/other/handoff.md
   ```
   The handoff records your git author name, so read it before sharing outside the team.

## If something goes wrong

If state was never saved, or a file is damaged, these are the manual repairs.

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `has a resume point but no state file` | the state file was deleted | run `mugiwara savepoint <mission> [handle] <flow>` to write it again, or delete the stale `continue-<handle>.json` |
| `✗ .mugiwara/missions/crew1/jane-doe.json: not valid JSON` from `continue`, `status`, `cost` or `archive` | a truncated or hand-edited state file; the command exits 1 | run the printed `fix:` line (restore from git, or delete the file and the next savepoint rewrites it). `mugiwara doctor` lists every bad file |
| `No mission in flight. Start one with Flow 0 triage` | nothing on disk for you | check your branch, or run `mugiwara continue --all` on a shared checkout |

## What you end up with

Either a printed resume point (mission, handle, stage, tasks, lane, next action) that you execute against the plan, or a `handoff.md` the next engineer reads first.

# Runbook: Review a mission's report

A teammate opened a pull request and attached a `report.md` from the crew. You have ten minutes and no wish to read the whole diff cold. This page tells you where the report helps, where it cannot, and what to push back on.

**When to use this:** you review a pull request that carries `.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/report.md`.
**Time:** 10 minutes for the report, then your normal review of the diff.
**You need:** the branch checked out, and the author available for questions.

## Steps

1. Open the report. It sits at `.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/report.md` and starts with a summary, the branch and the sensitive paths touched. This is an excerpt from a throwaway repo, where the mission trail was written by hand to demonstrate `archive`:
   ```markdown
   # Mission: rbac

   3 files changed (+13 / -0) on branch `feat/rbac`, closed 2026-10-19. Sensitive paths touched: `src/auth/rbac.js`, `test/rbac.test.js`.

   ## Verdict

   **Ready for review.** The recorded checks passed.
   ...
   ## Not verified

   Nothing was left unverified.

   ## Cost

   Used **20,694** of 50,000 tokens (41%).
   ```
   Do not stop at the verdict. In this demo the gates note says the repo gate failed because two tests already failed, yet the verdict line says ready and "Not verified" says nothing. (Current versions of `archive` no longer write a ready verdict without evidence.) A real report can disagree with itself the same way, so read every section.
2. Go through the checklist:
   - **Verdict.** One of Ready for review, Needs fixes, or Not enough evidence, and who decided. Anything but Ready needs a stated reason in the PR, not silence.
   - **Not verified.** Everything listed is now your job. An empty section on a large change deserves a question.
   - **Evidence.** Each check should name the command that ran and its result, such as a test command with its exit code. A claim without a command is a claim.
   - **Independent or inline review.** The first line of the Review and Security sections reads `Checked independently` or `Checked inline`. A hook writes it from a record of real subagent dispatches; the crew does not. Independent means a fresh-context subagent read the diff. Inline means the same model that wrote the code reviewed it. With no label, assume inline. The label proves a separate agent ran. It does not prove the review was good. Also check the order: stage order is not enforced, and a plan written after the build can satisfy the artifact check. Compare the file times of `plan.md` and the build's work; a plan newer than the code is a tell.
   - **Sensitive paths.** Read those files in the diff first. The report also ranks a reading order.
   - **Deferred items.** Each one needs an owner and a place it is tracked.
   - **Cost.** Compare the tokens used with the lane budget. A mission far over budget usually looped on a failing check.
3. Open `provenance.md` next to the report. It is the block the author should have pasted into the PR description:
   ```
   mission: rbac
   agent: Demo · model(s): unknown · lane full · mode guided
   tasks: 0/0
   gates/evidence: .mugiwara/missions/rbac/flows/01-execution.md · .mugiwara/missions/rbac/flows/03-quality.md · .mugiwara/missions/rbac/flows/04-gates.md
   branch: feat/rbac
   human review: pending (PR review is the terminal gate)
   ```
   *Real output from a throwaway repo (shortened). Note `tasks: 0/0` and `model(s): unknown`: the block records what was written to state, not what you would hope. The lane and mode tell you how much process ran.*
4. Spot-check one claim. Pick the test count in the report, run the suite, and compare.
5. Leave your comments on the pull request, not in the report. The report records what the author's session did.

## Red flags

- No evidence: the mission declares no checks. The closing step prints this warning when it happens:
  ```
  closure integrity warnings (non-blocking):
    ✗ [evidence] mission declares no evidence — closing with zero recorded checks
  ```
  *Real output from `mugiwara archive`. It does not block, so a zero-check report can still be attached.*
- A report of a few hand-written lines. The author probably had no global CLI, so `archive` never ran and nothing was folded. Ask them to install it and archive.
- A "Needs fixes" or "Not enough evidence" verdict that was ignored. The PR says "ready" and the report does not.
- The verdict contradicts a section, as in the demo above.
- `Checked inline` on a change that touches auth, payments or a migration. Check `independent_review` is not `off` and that you ran on Claude Code. If it was off by choice, the extra checking is yours: read the sensitive files line by line.
- Sensitive paths in the diff that the report does not list.
- "Not verified" is empty on a change with no end-to-end tests.
- A deferred item with no owner.

## What to ask the author

- Which of the checks in the report did you re-run yourself?
- Why does a sensitive change say `Checked inline`: host, lane, or `independent_review=off`?
- Which tests were already failing on main, and where are they tracked?
- What is in "Not verified" that you plan to test before merge?
- Did the crew block any command, and what did you run by hand instead?

## If something goes wrong

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| there is no `report.md` in the branch | the mission was never closed, or the trail was not committed | ask the author to run `mugiwara archive <mission>` and commit the result |
| the report is only a short note | the global CLI was missing | ask the author to install it and archive again |
| you cannot tell who approved what | the mission ran in guided mode without notes | read `decisions.md` if it is still there, or ask |

## What you end up with

A short list of questions for the author and a clear idea of which parts of the diff the report covers and which it does not. The report speeds up a review. It does not replace one.

# Runbook: Run a risky change (auth, payments, migrations)

A login change that ships with "tests pass" and nothing else is how a Friday night starts. This runbook covers the changes where you want a plan, a security pass and a written verdict, and it says plainly which parts you still have to check yourself.

**When to use this:** the change touches `auth/`, payments or billing, secrets, CI, a migration or schema file, or nine or more files.
**Time:** 20 to 60 minutes in guided mode. Less in auto mode, but you review more at the end.
**You need:** the crew installed with the global CLI (see [your first mission](solo-mission.md)), a clean working tree, and the tests passing on your branch or a list of the ones that already fail.

## Steps

1. Start on a branch and say what you want in one sentence, with the rules that matter.
   ```text
   /mugiwara add role-based access control: admin, editor, viewer
   ```
   Paths such as `auth/`, payments, migrations, secrets and CI always size the work as the full lane, whatever the file count. The full lane is the one that runs a plan, an audit, quality and coverage gates, a review, a security pass and a fix loop.
2. Expect questions before any code. In guided mode the crew stops and asks. For the request above it asked six, shortened here (an excerpt, not the full reply):
   ```text
   1. Where does identity come from: an IdP or JWT, a local user store, or the caller passes a role?
   2. Which resources are protected?
   3. What do the roles mean? My default: admin does everything, editor reads and writes, viewer reads.
   4. Where is it enforced?
   5. Are the roles fixed or editable?
   6. Solo or shared?
   Reply with answers or "use your defaults".
   ```
   Answer the ones where your system has a fact the crew cannot see: where identity comes from and which resources count. Take its defaults for the rest only if you read them first. A default is a guess, and in security work a guess about role meaning is the most expensive kind.
3. Pick the mode. Guided mode waits for you at each decision. That suits a risky change, because you see the plan before code exists. To run to the end instead, set `mode=auto` in `.mugiwara/config` or say `mugiwara mode auto` in the chat. In auto mode the crew still stops for a real blocker or when a failed check has used up its fix rounds.
4. Read the plan when it appears. Check that the acceptance checks would actually fail if the feature were wrong. Ask for changes now: this is the cheap moment.
5. Watch the state while it builds.
   ```bash
   mugiwara status
   ```
   ```
   rbac
     flow 1 · 0/0 tasks · lane full (sensitive paths: src/auth/rbac.js,test/rbac.test.js) · mode guided
     blockers 0 · heal cycle 1/3 · files touched 3
     tokens 20580/50000 (ok)
     branch feat/rbac · updated 2026-10-19T05:05:06Z
   ```
   *Real output from a throwaway repo (v1.0.5). `heal cycle 1/3` means the fix loop is allowed three rounds.*
6. When it closes, open `report.md` and read it as a reviewer would, with [review a mission](review-a-mission.md). Then do your own checks from the list below.

## What you will see on Claude Code

- **The reminder and the hold.** If `/mugiwara <request>` names a risk area, a prompt hook reminds the model to take the full process. If the change is risky and no mission was recorded, or review files are missing, or the review ran inline, the stop hook blocks the end of the turn and the model continues. This happens at most twice a session, then it becomes a warning. Only `enforce=off` turns it off.
- **The closure refusal.** On the full lane or a sensitive path, `mugiwara archive` refuses to close if the ledger shows no separate run of both Robin and Jinbe. The message names the missing check. Either run it as a separate agent and archive again, or set `independent_review=off`. `archive --force` closes anyway and the report says `Checked inline`.
- **The cost.** The report's Cost section shows the process estimate against budget and the provider-reported tokens on a separate line. Independent review costs more: see [cost](../concepts/cost.md).

## What each stage leaves in `.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/`

- Plan stage: `plan.md` and, when the idea was vague, `spec.md`.
- Build stage: `flows/01-execution.md`, a task table with the evidence for each task.
- Check, quality and gate stages: `flows/02-audit.md`, `03-quality.md`, `04-gates.md`.
- Review and security stages: `review.md` and `security.md`.
- Fix stage, only when a check failed: `flows/05-healing.md`.
- Decisions and blockers as they happen: `decisions.md`, `blockers.md`.
- Closing: `report.md`, `pr-verdict.md`, `rollback.sh`, `provenance.md`.

After `mugiwara archive <mission>` the loose files are folded into `report.md` and removed. What stays:

```
plan.md
provenance.md
report.md
rollback.sh
```

*Real listing of a closed mission in a throwaway repo. The trail there was written by hand to demonstrate `archive`, so a real mission may keep more files, such as `pr-verdict.md`.*

## What you still verify yourself

On Claude Code, a full-lane or sensitive-path mission runs Robin and Jinbe as separate subagents (`independent_review=on`), and the report says `Checked independently`. That is a second read by a fresh context, and it still does not replace your checks. When the report says `Checked inline`, the same model that wrote the code read it again: treat that review as a checklist the author filled in, not a second opinion.

- Run the test suite yourself and compare it with the count in the report.
- Read the diff of every sensitive path line by line. The report lists them.
- For auth: try the denied case by hand. The role that should not get in, the expired token, the missing header.
- For migrations: run the rollback on a copy of the data before you trust it.
- For payments or secrets: check that no key, token or card number landed in the diff, the logs or the tests.
- Read "Not verified". Anything listed there is yours.
- Check pre-existing failures. The crew flags a test that was already failing so it is not blamed on the change. Confirm that on main.

## When to stop and take over

- The report says Needs fixes and the reason is about your change, not a failure that was already there. Fix it by hand or ask for a new mission.
- The same check fails after the third fix round. The crew stops and hands you the history. More rounds will not help.
- The crew is asking the same question twice, or its defaults keep contradicting what you told it.
- A command was blocked by the guard. The crew never merges, deploys or force-pushes. Run that step yourself, see [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).
- The diff is larger than your plan. Stop, trim the scope, and start a smaller mission.

## If something goes wrong

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| it built code without asking | the mode is `auto`, or the request was specific enough | read the plan and decisions in the trail, then review as usual |
| no security pass shows in the report | the change did not touch a sensitive path | say `Jinbe, audit the auth middleware` in the chat to ask for one |
| Needs fixes on the repo, ready on the change | tests that already failed on main | confirm on main, then record the failing tests as a deferred item with an owner |
| the lane is full but the change is two lines | a sensitive path was touched | expected. Ask for a smaller process only if you accept the risk |

## What you end up with

An uncommitted change in your tree, a closed mission with a verdict, and a report that says what was and was not checked. The next step is yours: your own checks, your commit, your pull request.

# Runbook: Your first mission

You installed the crew, typed a small request, and nothing visibly changed. That is expected, and this page shows what a request that does engage the crew looks like, so you can tell the two apart.

**When to use this:** you work alone and want one change reviewed properly, with a report you can attach to a pull request.
**Time:** 10 to 30 minutes, mostly spent answering questions.
**You need:** a git repo with one commit, Claude Code or opencode, and a change worth reviewing: auth, payments, a migration, or anything that touches many files.

## Steps

1. Install the crew into the repo. On Claude Code you can use the two `/plugin` commands from the [install page](../install.md) instead.
   ```bash
   mugiwara install --target claude --yes
   ```
   ```
   default .mugiwara/config written at <project>/.mugiwara/config (edit it to customise)

   -> Claude Code (project)
      written 115, skipped 0, backed up 0
      note: hooks registered in <project>/.claude/settings.json

   OK mugiwara 1.0.5 installed (manifest: <project>/.mugiwara/manifest.json)
   2 note(s) above may need attention.
   CLI: run `npm i -g @ionivetech/mugiwara` so the crew can call `mugiwara savepoint/archive/continue` directly.
        Without it the crew falls back to npx, then `.mugiwara/bin/*.sh`, then direct file ops — state and resume keep working.
   ```
   The files appear as untracked in `git status`: a `.claude/` folder, a `.mugiwara/` folder, and an edit to `.gitignore`.
2. Install the CLI once on your machine, as the note says: `npm i -g @ionivetech/mugiwara`. Do not skip this. Without it the crew falls back to shell scripts, never runs `archive`, and the closing report is a short hand-written note instead of the folded one.
3. Pick the change. Choose something you would want a second pair of eyes on, such as role-based access control or a signup validation change. A one-line fix will not exercise the crew, see "A small change runs direct" below.
4. In the chat, run the command with your request:
   ```text
   /mugiwara add role-based access control: admin, editor, viewer
   ```
   The crew sizes the work from the diff and the paths involved. Access control touches security, so it picks the full pipeline (called a lane; the lanes are Direct, Lean, Standard, Full and Spike). It names its members in one line, then stops before writing code and asks numbered questions. This is an excerpt of a real first reply, shortened:
   ```text
   Access control touches security, so this gets the full pipeline. Mode is guided, so I need
   your go at each stage. I'm stopping before any code because the request is too vague to plan.
   ...
   1. Where does identity come from: an IdP or JWT, a local user store, or the caller passes a role?
   2. Which resources are protected: only invoices, or more?
   3. What do the roles mean? My default: admin does everything, editor reads and writes, viewer reads.
   ...
   Reply with answers or "use your defaults".
   ```
   It may also point out a failing test that has nothing to do with your request, so the failure is not blamed on this work.
5. Answer, or reply `use your defaults`. In the default guided mode the crew then waits for your reply at each decision. That is slow on purpose. To let it run to the end, set `mode=auto` in `.mugiwara/config`, or say `mugiwara mode auto` in the chat.
6. Check where the mission is, from a terminal in the repo.
   ```bash
   mugiwara status
   ```
   ```
   rbac
     flow 1 · 0/0 tasks · lane full (sensitive paths: src/auth/rbac.js,test/rbac.test.js) · mode guided
     blockers 0 · heal cycle 1/3 · files touched 3
     tokens 20580/50000 (ok)
     branch feat/rbac · updated 2026-10-19T05:05:06Z
   ```
   *Real output from a throwaway repo (v1.0.5), after a state save at the first stage. The token figure is the process estimate described in [cost](../concepts/cost.md).*
7. See what the mission cost.
   ```bash
   mugiwara cost
   ```
   ```
   Tokens: process estimate 20694 · no provider usage recorded
   Cost envelope: ok 41% (20694/50000)
   Avoided: 0 stages, 0 contexts, ~0 tokens
   Efficiency: reuse 0, dup 0 chars, budget 41%
   Forced continuations (Stop hook blocks): 0
   Trail: 0 decisions
   ```
   On Claude Code the Stop hook also records the provider-reported token total of the session. When it has, `mugiwara cost` prints it next to the estimate. Here no session was recorded, so it says so.
8. When the crew finishes, it closes the mission and writes `.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/report.md`. By default (`auto_commit=off`) your tree stays uncommitted and the crew prints the git commands for you to run. It never opens a pull request, merges or deploys.
9. Read the report before you attach it. The verdict, the "Not verified" section and the evidence table matter most. A reviewer will read them first, see [review a mission](review-a-mission.md).

## A small change runs direct

Type `/mugiwara fix the typo in the invoice header` and the crew will most likely decide it is a one-line fix, say so, and make the change. There is no mission and no report. That is the design: a typo should not cost a pipeline. To force the full crew on something small, ask for it: `/mugiwara <request>, use the full crew`.

A plain request with no `/mugiwara` usually does not engage the crew at all. In a test, "fix the date format bug in the invoice list" produced no skill call, no mission and no report, the same as an agent without Mugiwara. If you want the crew, start with the slash command.

## If something goes wrong

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| no mission, no report | the request was small or had no `/mugiwara` | run `/mugiwara <request>`, add "use the full crew" if it is small |
| the crew keeps asking for your go | guided mode waits at each decision | reply, or set `mode=auto` |
| `report.md` is a few hand-written lines | the global CLI is missing, so `archive` did not run | `npm i -g @ionivetech/mugiwara`, then `mugiwara archive <mission>` |
| `mugiwara: command not found` | the CLI is not on PATH | `npx -y @ionivetech/mugiwara@latest <command>` |
| `mugiwara status` prints `No mission state on disk.` | no mission started in this checkout | check the branch and that you used `/mugiwara` |

More messages and fixes: [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md). For auth, payments and migrations, read [risky change](risky-change.md) next.

## What you end up with

Uncommitted code and tests in your tree, and `.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/` holding `report.md`, `plan.md` (when the lane wrote one), `provenance.md` and `rollback.sh`. Commit the report with your change. Most of the crew runs inside your conversation, so its reviews are the same model checking its own work unless the report says otherwise.

# Runbook: Team mission, lead plus handles

Three people editing one plan collide unless each owns a named slice. The lead cuts the work into owned areas, then each person (a handle, such as `jane-doe`) runs their own slice and branch. The same steps cover someone joining a mission already in flight.

**When to use this:** work splits across named people with separate areas and branches.
**Time:** about 15 minutes of lead setup, then minutes per stage.
**You need:** a git repo, the crew installed, and one lowercase slug per person.

The outputs below come from a real run in a throwaway repo (v1.0.5).

## Lead

1. Cut a branch and describe the split in chat, naming each handle and area. Example: `jane-doe` owns api, `john-smith` owns web.
2. Write one row per handle in the plan's `## Sub-missions` table. The header is `| ID | Name | Assignee | Branch | Status | Depends On | Touched Files |`. Then check that no file belongs to two rows.
   ```bash
   mugiwara plan conflict-check .mugiwara/missions/crew1/plan.md
   ```
   ```
   no conflicts: no file is touched by two sub-missions
   ```
3. Commit the plan and push the branch so everyone starts from the same file.

## Each handle

4. Pull, then resume. With several handles you get a numbered picker. Pass your handle next time to skip it.
   ```bash
   mugiwara continue crew1
   ```
   ```
   Mission: crew1

     #  ID  AREA           ASSIGNEE  STATE
     1  S1  api            jane-doe  Flow 2
     2  S2  web            john-smith Flow 2

   Which one are you? [1-2]
   ```
   ```bash
   mugiwara continue crew1 jane-doe
   ```
   ```
   Resumed: crew1 [jane-doe], Flow 2, 0/0 tasks — next_action: verify this flow stage against the plan, then continue per plan (next stage or closure) — run: (no next_session_prompt recorded)
   ```
5. Work your stage. The crew saves your position as you go, under your own handle, so nobody overwrites anyone else.

## Joining a mission already in flight

6. Pull, then join with your handle and area. This adds a row to the plan, logs the join in `decisions.md` and sets you as the active handle.
   ```bash
   mugiwara join crew1 sophia-martinez --area testing
   ```
   ```
   joined crew1 as sophia-martinez (testing) — plan updated, decisions logged, active-member set
   ```
   Read your new row and the rows around it so your slice does not collide. Then continue as in step 4.

## Closing

7. Every handle must reach the last stage. Then the lead runs `mugiwara archive crew1`. Until then closure refuses and says who is still working:
   ```
   mugiwara: closure blocked — mission "crew1" is not finished:
     jane-doe     Flow 2, still in flight
     john-smith   Flow 2, still in flight
     sophia-martinez Flow 3, still in flight

     Every assignee must reach Flow 9. Run `mugiwara status` to check.
     Use --force to archive anyway — in-flight resume points will be lost.
   ```

## If something goes wrong

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `refusing to add member 'jane-doe'` | the mission started solo | `mugiwara migrate --to-team jane-doe` |
| `member "x" already in roster` | the handle joined twice | `mugiwara continue crew1 x` and work |
| `no plan for mission "crew1"` | the mission never wrote `plan.md` | ask the lead for the plan, or start from triage |
| `no sub-mission table found in plan.md` | the plan has no sub-missions table | the lead adds it, then you join again |
| `invalid member name "bad name!"` | spaces or a reserved word in the handle | use a slug such as `sophia-martinez` |
| closure blocked, `assigned, never started` | a roster row has no state | that person runs `mugiwara continue crew1 <handle>` |

## What you end up with

`.mugiwara/missions/crew1/` holds one state file and one resume file per handle, a shared `plan.md` with the sub-missions table, and, after closure, one `report.md` covering everyone.

# Runbook: Troubleshooting common failures

The crew did not start, a report came out thin, or a command failed with a message you do not recognize. Find the symptom below, apply the fix, and run it again.

**When to use this:** something did not happen, or a `mugiwara` command errors.
**Time:** about 2 minutes per symptom.
**You need:** the failing command or the chat reply, and its full output.

## Steps

1. Read the whole message. Most print the fix. With nothing on disk, even the empty state tells you the next move:
   ```bash
   mugiwara continue
   ```
   ```
   No mission in flight. Start one with Flow 0 triage (mugiwara-orchestration).
   ```
2. If the crew did not do what you expected, check these first.
   - **The crew did not engage.** A plain request with no `/mugiwara` gets your agent's normal behavior. Run `/mugiwara <request>, use the full crew` when you want it.
   - **The report is a few hand-written lines.** The global CLI is missing, so `archive` never ran. Run `npm i -g @ionivetech/mugiwara`, then `mugiwara archive <mission>`.
   - **The crew keeps waiting for you.** Guided mode asks at each decision. Reply, set `mode=auto` in `.mugiwara/config`, or say `mugiwara mode auto` in the chat.
   - **A hook warns about triage.** The Stop hook saw changed code with no mission to size it. Default `enforce=warn` prints:
     ```
     ⚠ Mugiwara: this session changed source or mission artifacts but no mission was started to size the work. Start the mugiwara workflow first (it also records trivial work), or set enforce=off in .mugiwara/config to stop this check.
     ```
     Start the work with `/mugiwara <request>`. With `enforce=block` the hook stops the turn instead of warning, and the stop is counted in `mugiwara cost` as a forced continuation.
   - **The turn was blocked after `/mugiwara`.** The stop hook compared the real diff with what happened: the change is risky and no mission, review or security file was recorded. Let the crew continue and run the process. It blocks at most twice per session, then warns.
   - **`mugiwara archive` refused to close.** On the full lane or a sensitive path, the ledger shows no independent run of Robin and Jinbe. The message names the missing check. Run it as a separate agent and archive again, or set `independent_review=off`, or use `--force` (the report then says `Checked inline`). Hosts without the Claude Code ledger are not blocked.
   - **A hook warns that the review was not independent.** The Stop hook found a full-lane or sensitive-path mission with `review.md` or `security.md` and no recorded subagent dispatch, so the review ran inline. Causes: `independent_review=off`, a host that cannot dispatch, or a skipped dispatch. Re-run review on Claude Code with `independent_review=on`, or check the inline review yourself. It only warns.
   - **A command was blocked.** The guard refuses merges, deploys, pushes to a protected branch and other irreversible commands on Claude Code. A real refusal for `git push origin main`:
     ```
     {"decision":"block","reason":"Mugiwara blocked this command (pushing to a protected branch), because the crew never creates a PR, merges or deploys; a human does. Run it yourself, or set enforce=off in .mugiwara/config."}
     ```
     Run that command in your own terminal.
   - **A savepoint rejects a name.** Mission and member names allow letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore, and may not start with a dash:
     ```
     savepoint: invalid mission name "bad name" (allowlist: [a-zA-Z0-9._-])
     savepoint: invalid member name "-x" (allowlist: [a-zA-Z0-9._-])
     ```
     *Real output from the installed `.mugiwara/bin/savepoint.sh`.* In the shell script, put the mission first and the flags after it: `savepoint.sh <mission> --flow 2`. A flag before the mission is rejected as an unknown flag.
   - **Why the crew did not engage, in detail.** Run `mugiwara doctor` first; it reports what it finds. The usual causes:
     - Mode: `mode` in `.mugiwara/config` sets how much the crew asks. Guided waits at each decision.
     - Small-request direct path: a trivial request is answered directly, with no mission.
     - Risk reminder: on a risky change the hook asks for a mission. It is a reminder, not an error.
     - Mugiwara off: `mugiwara off` in chat stands the crew down for the session. Start again with `/mugiwara <request>`.
3. For a message from a command, find it in the table and apply the fix.
4. Run the command again. If the message changed, match it again from the top.

## If something goes wrong

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `refusing to add member 'jane-doe'` | a solo mission (`state.json`) was given a handle | `mugiwara migrate --to-team jane-doe` |
| `has a resume point but no state file` | an orphaned resume file | `mugiwara savepoint <mission> [handle] <flow>`, or delete `.mugiwara/missions/<m>/continue-<handle>.json` |
| `closure blocked`, naming an unfinished mission | someone is still below the last stage | finish every handle, or `archive --force` and accept that resume points are lost |
| `has state but no sub-mission in plan.md` | a handle started without a roster row | `mugiwara join <mission> <handle> --area <area>`, or fix the spelling |
| `savepoint: not a git repository` | ran outside a git repo | `git init`, make one commit, retry |
| `closure integrity gate failed` from `mugiwara archive` | a missing file link, a secret-shaped string, or a bad evidence path | fix the flagged file and archive again. There is no bypass flag |
| `invalid member name "x"` | spaces, a leading dash or a reserved word | use a slug such as `grace-hopper` |
| `conflict (not overwritten; run update to replace with backup)` from install | the target file differs from what install writes | `mugiwara update`, which backs up first |
| `✗ …/state.json: not valid JSON` or `mission dir is empty` | a truncated mission file | run the printed `fix:` line. `mugiwara doctor` lists all |
| `No mission state on disk.` | nothing recorded in this checkout | check the branch, or start with `/mugiwara <request>` |
| `multiple missions on disk … specify <mission>` | the short form cannot tell which mission | pass the mission: `mugiwara savepoint --flow 2 <mission>` |
| no crew banner in the chat | the crew is not loaded in this session | ask "which crew members are available?". If it cannot answer, reinstall: see [install](../install.md) |
| `no per-commit note` from `handoff --path` | git notes are not fetched by clone | see [signing and provenance](../optional/signing.md) |

To see what the stop hook receives, run the host with `MUGIWARA_HOOK_DEBUG=<file>`: it appends one line per stop (event, whether it was already a continuation, pending mission).

## What you end up with

Either a clean re-run or a narrower error. When two symptoms overlap, fix a corrupt state file before roster issues, because a corrupt file hides the roster.

# Runbook: Upgrade, clean up, uninstall

A new release landed, or you want the crew out of a repo, and you do not want to lose a mission that is still in flight. This page covers the five commands that change what is installed or what is on disk, and what each one leaves alone.

**When to use this:** you update the package, tidy up old missions, or remove Mugiwara from a repo.
**Time:** 5 minutes.
**You need:** the global CLI, and a clean `git status` so you can see what changed.

## Upgrade

1. Update the package, then check what is installed against what the CLI would write.
   ```bash
   mugiwara list --check
   ```
   ```
   project: v1.0.5 targets=claude files=115 missing=0 stale=0 installed=2026-10-19T05:04:33.716Z
   ```
   `missing` counts installed files that are gone, `stale` counts files that no longer match.
2. Read the GitHub release notes for what you must change. For 2.0: old `features=` tokens still work, `eval-runner` moved to `evals/agents/`, and `coverage_new` and `coverage_modified` can become `coverage=<n>`. `flows/` file names and the `.mugiwara/` layout are unchanged.
3. Refresh the installed copies.
   ```bash
   mugiwara update --target claude --yes
   ```
   ```
   -> Claude Code (project)
      written 5, skipped 93, backed up 1
      note: existing command kept: <project>/.claude/commands/mugiwara-review.md
      note: existing command kept: <project>/.claude/commands/mugiwara-continue.md
      note: existing command kept: <project>/.claude/commands/mugiwara.md
      note: existing command kept: <project>/.claude/commands/mugiwara-security.md

   OK mugiwara 1.0.5 installed (manifest: <project>/.mugiwara/manifest.json)
   ```
   *Real output, shortened. In this run one agent file had a local edit and one was deleted. Update wrote the missing file, replaced the edited one, and kept a copy of the edit under `.mugiwara/backup/<timestamp>-claude/`. Command files that already exist are kept as they are, so your own changes to `/mugiwara` survive an update.*
4. Run `mugiwara list --check` again. It should report `missing=0 stale=0`. Then run `mugiwara doctor`. If it says `installed command pins older version`, delete `.claude/commands/mugiwara.md` and run `mugiwara update` again: update keeps that file, so the old npx pin stays until you do.

## What happens to missions in flight

Nothing. `update` does not touch `.mugiwara/missions/`, `.mugiwara/config` or your lessons file. The files under `flows/NN-*.md` keep their names on purpose, so a mission started before the upgrade resumes the same way. Check with `mugiwara continue`, see [resume after a crash](resume-after-crash.md).

If your `features=` line in `.mugiwara/config` names an old skill, it still works as an alias for the new one. You can rename at your own pace.

## Tidy up old missions

5. Fold every closed mission into its report in one go.
   ```bash
   mugiwara clean
   ```
   ```
   closure integrity warnings (non-blocking):
     ✗ [evidence] mission declares no evidence — closing with zero recorded checks
   cleaned rbac → missions/rbac/report.md
   index updated: index.md
   ```
   `clean` skips missions that still have live state. `--include-live` includes them, but it still refuses until you add `--force`:
   ```
   ✗ in-flight mission(s): live1. Use --force to archive them anyway.
   ```
   Archiving a live mission throws away its resume point. `--stale <date>` also picks up missions untouched since that date.

## Wipe mission state

6. Start over without losing what the team learned:
   ```bash
   mugiwara reset --keep-logs
   ```
   ```
   ✗ Active mission for '<git author>'. Use --force to override.
   ```
   *The real message prints your git name. `reset` refuses while you have a mission in flight and exits 1.* With `--force`:
   ```
   removed: missions, index.md
   kept: lessons.md, config, manifest.json
   ```
   Plain `reset --force` also removes `lessons.md`. Reset deletes mission folders, including reports you never committed. Commit what you want to keep first.

## Uninstall

7. Remove the installed files with the manifest as the list.
   ```bash
   mugiwara uninstall --yes
   ```
   ```
   Will remove 115 files (targets: claude).
      unwired mugiwara hooks from <project>/.claude/settings.json
      note: .gitignore stripped mugiwara block
   OK removed 115 files
   ```
   Without `--yes` it asks `Proceed? [y/N]` first.
8. Check `.claude/settings.json`. Uninstall removes only Mugiwara's hook entries (in a throwaway repo, v1.0.5, your own hooks and permissions stayed). The file itself stays, `{}` if it held nothing else.
9. Decide what to do with `.mugiwara/`. Uninstall leaves `config`, `lessons.md`, `missions/`, `backup/` and the review ledger `review-dispatch.jsonl`. Your reports are yours, so keep them or delete the folder.

## If something goes wrong

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `mugiwara: command not found` | the global CLI is not installed | `npm i -g @ionivetech/mugiwara`, or run `npx -y @ionivetech/mugiwara@latest <command>` |
| `✗ in-flight mission(s)` from `clean` | a mission still has live state | finish it, or pass `--force` and lose its resume point |
| `doctor` says the command pins an older version | `update` keeps an existing `.claude/commands/mugiwara.md` | delete it, run `mugiwara update` |
| `doctor` says `pipeline-guard.js is not wired to Stop` | an older CLI install ran the guard only for subagents, so nothing checked the main session at stop | run `mugiwara update --target claude` |

## What you end up with

An installed crew that matches the package, or a repo without it. Missions in flight keep their names, state and resume points. Reports stay on disk until you remove them.

# Eval-Runner — Test Engineer (for the Harness)

## Before you start

Run the entry checks and open with the banner: `_shared/references/agent-protocol.md`, `_shared/references/flow-banners.md`. EvalRunner tests the harness, not a mission, so the no-mission triage step does not apply; if a mission is named, its state, plan, and blockers must exist, otherwise stop and report what is missing.

## Role

Test engineer for the harness itself. Writes task suites, runs them, judges rubric comparisons, and reports pass or fail per case. Verifies that skills and agents work. Files failures and never fixes the skill under test.

## Experience

Harness test engineer who files failures and leaves the fix to others. Abilities: rubric judging, the fresh-judge rule, honest pass/fail tables, catching skill rot before it ships.

## When dispatched

- After a skill change lands.
- Before release, as a full-suite run.
- On demand by Luffy to prove a skill or agent works.
- When skill rot is suspected (behavior drifts from the skill's description).

## Rules

1. Follow `docs/contributing/evals.md`: suite format, judge protocol, loop, bound.
2. At least one case per skill; a full suite run per release.
3. Judge with a fresh agent, never the implementer of the case's skill.
4. A failing case is filed to the ledger and goes to Brook for the fix. EvalRunner never fixes the skill and never edits the eval to make it pass.
5. Write the pass/fail table to `.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/flows/eval.md`.
6. Write failures to `.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/blockers.md` (category `eval-fail`); recommend: Brook.
7. Ranking or selection cases use tournament judging (`mugiwara-checkpoint` adversarial depth): pairwise, fresh judge per match.
8. Never assert on host-agent behavior; check only that the skill's instructions produce the intended workflow.

## Output

Pass/fail table with evidence in `.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/flows/eval.md`, summarized inline. Failing cases go to the ledger; recommend: Brook.

## Return to Luffy

Output goes to Luffy; recommend a next step, never hand off or dispatch another crew member (`_shared/references/agent-protocol.md`).

## Red flags

- Scoring a case with no rubric or pass threshold.
- The implementer judging its own skill.
- An eval edited to clear a failure.
- A suite run with no report written.
- Judging host-agent runtime behavior as a skill failure.
- Unbounded re-runs to "try to pass".

All mean: the run is invalid. Re-run clean, then report.

# Database — raw SQL and ORM

Applies whenever the diff touches a query, migration, model, or repository.
The repo's existing data layer wins: if it uses an ORM, write ORM; if it uses
raw SQL with a thin helper, write that. Never introduce a second data layer.

## Choosing per change

| Situation | Reach for |
|-----------|-----------|
| CRUD against one or two tables, relations mapped | the repo's ORM |
| Reporting/aggregation, bulk update, window functions | raw SQL (parameterized) through the repo's query helper |
| Hot path measured slow under the ORM | raw SQL for that query only — note why inline |
| Schema change | a migration file, never ad-hoc DDL |

## Non-negotiables (either style)

- **Parameterized queries only.** String-concatenated SQL is a blocker-level
  security finding. ORM query builders parameterize by default — do not
  defeat them with `raw()` string interpolation of user input.
- **Constraints live in the schema**: unique, not-null, FK, check. App-level
  validation is UX; the database is the guarantee.
- **Transactions around every multi-row write.** Partial writes are data
  loss. One request = one transaction boundary, not several.
- **Migrations are forward-only files** with a documented rollback statement.
  No editing an applied migration; add a new one.

## Concurrency

- Know the isolation level you run at (read committed is typical). Do not
  reach for serializable to paper over a logic race.
- Lost-update protection: optimistic locking (version column) unless the row
  is a single-writer counter.
- Deadlocks: consistent lock ordering across the codebase; keep transactions
  short — no network calls inside one.

## ORM pitfalls

- **N+1 from lazy loading**: a loop touching `order.customer.name` issues one
  query per iteration. Eager-load (`include`/`joinedload`/`select_related`)
  what the loop renders.
- **Implicit transactions**: some ORMs wrap each save in its own commit — a
  "transaction" spread across three saves was never atomic.
- **Mass assignment**: bind request bodies through explicit field allowlists,
  not `Model(**payload)`.
- **Silent full-table scans**: check the generated SQL for anything the ORM
  could not translate (client-side filtering after fetch).

## Raw-SQL pitfalls

- Unparameterized interpolation (see above) and dynamic ORDER BY/LIMIT built
  from user input — whitelist column names instead.
- Missing LIMIT on list queries; pagination is not optional.
- Long-running transactions holding locks while the app does other work.

## Indexes

Index the columns every hot WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY actually uses — verify with
EXPLAIN on the real query shape, not by intuition. A new query pattern on a
large table without a matching index is a performance finding, same severity
as an N+1.

# Stack-specific notes (apply only if the repo uses it)

These are examples for two common stacks. Use a section only when the dependency file shows that stack, and check the docs for the installed version first (`_shared/references/source-grounding.md`). Version numbers below are unverified against your repo.

## Prisma (ORM)

- Multi-row writes go in one interactive transaction (`prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => { ... })`); a throw rolls everything back. Set explicit transaction timeouts rather than relying on defaults.
- One `PrismaClient` per process. In hot-reload dev, cache it on `globalThis`; a client per request leaks connections.
- Avoid N+1: load relations with `include` or `select` in one query, never loop-query a relation.
- Index columns used by hot WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY clauses (`@@index([field])`); confirm with EXPLAIN.
- A concurrent write on a unique column throws error code P2002 (`PrismaClientKnownRequestError`). Catch it, then retry or map to 409; a bare 500 hides the race.

Docs: https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-client/queries/transactions, https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/reference/prisma-client-reference

## Express (HTTP)

- Do not render errors in the route. Call `next(err)` and let one central error middleware respond.
- The error middleware takes exactly four arguments `(err, req, res, next)` and is registered after all routes. It returns the repo's one error envelope (see `mugiwara-contract-first`, "Error envelope").
- Log each error with context (path, method, stack, trace id when tracing exists).
- Never leak stack traces or internals to clients.

Docs: https://expressjs.com/en/guide/error-handling.html

# Adversarial depth — doubt-driven verification inside the audit

One skill, two depths. The standard audit checks finished work; this pass verifies a decision while it
is still in-flight — when a wrong call costs minutes to catch and hours to
reverse. The default disposition of the decider is self-preferential: biased
toward its own conclusion. Doubt is the counterweight, and it works best in a
fresh context. Never validate. Find what is wrong.

## When to use (beyond the standard audit)

- High stakes: money, security, data, or a public contract at stake.
- Unfamiliar code: deciding inside a subsystem not traced end to end.
- Confident outputs: a plan, estimate, or verdict produced fast and asserted
  smoothly — cheaper to verify now than to discover wrong later.
- Before committing a decision other agents will build on.
- Skip when: cheap to reverse; already independently verified (fresh review,
  real test run, external check).

## Process — CLAIM → EXTRACT → DOUBT → RECONCILE → STOP, in order

### 1. CLAIM — state the decision

One falsifiable sentence: what is decided, what it promises. A claim you
cannot state is a claim you have not understood. Record who decided and when.

### 2. EXTRACT — pull the load-bearing facts

Break the claim into its smallest facts; a fact is load-bearing when the
claim fails if it is false. Facts are specific: function name, schema column,
ordering guarantee, latency budget, API contract, count. Name the artifact
and file. A claim on one unexamined assumption is unverified.

### 3. DOUBT — attack each fact, find what breaks

"What must be true for this to hold, and what breaks if not?" Attack from the
direction it would be wrong: edge inputs, empty states, concurrent calls,
upstream changes, naming collisions, contract drift, silent fallbacks. Do NOT
hunt confirmations. List every way the fact can be false first. Re-derive
from code and docs as if the claim never existed. Never skip DOUBT because
the claim feels right.

### 4. RECONCILE — verify against the source of truth

Check each doubted fact against actual code, docs, schema, measurements — not
the claim's summary. Classify: contract-misread, actionable, trade-off,
noise. Report the first three. Fix or reject. A surviving decision is not
"correct" — it is "still standing after the search."

### 5. STOP — cap at `heal_max_cycles` rounds, then escalate

After the cap the claim is reconciled or it is not. If not, STOP and escalate
with the unresolved claim — never restart and call it rigor.

## Rationalizations

| Rationalization | Truth |
| --- | --- |
| "It's obvious, no need to doubt" | Obviousness is a bias signal, not proof. |
| "The plan says so" | The plan is the claim, not the evidence. |
| "I'm just double-checking" | Confirming is validating. Stop. |

## Red flags (adversarial)

- Claim accepted without extracting load-bearing facts.
- A fact checked only in the confirming direction.
- Findings from the decider's own context, no fresh re-derivation.
- "Verified" without classification.
- Going past `heal_max_cycles` rounds instead of escalating.
- Editing code to "prove" a point — doubt finds, implementers fix.

## Verification output

Claim restated, facts extracted, each fact's doubt + reconcile outcome, round
count, escalate-or-resolve. The output is the doubt trail, not a verdict
paragraph. A decision with no doubt trail is unverified.

Not `mugiwara-review`: that reviews a finished diff adversarially. This
verifies a decision before the diff exists — different artifact, earlier
moment, same stance.

# Failure ledger (checkpoint)

Chopper appends one row per failing criterion to `.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/blockers.md`, creating it only if absent. Row schema, field meanings, and the categories (`test-fail`, `type-error`, `missing-impl`, `parallel-conflict`, `regression`, `flaky`, `env`): see the failure taxonomy in `mugiwara-healing`.

Checkpoint-specific rules:

- Every unmet acceptance criterion gets its own row, with the command that was re-run in `attempted`.
- An acceptance criterion with no command or file to check gives no evidence and is unverifiable: file it as `missing-impl`, do not waive it.
- `env` needs a clean-checkout reproduction. Without it, file `test-fail`.
- A check that passes sometimes and fails sometimes is `flaky`: run it 3 times, put all three results in `attempted`, and name an owner in `help-needed`.

Example:

```
| 4 | T5 | missing-impl: no thumbnail endpoint | searched routes/, not found | endpoint may sit in a later plan task |
```

# Contract-First Process

## 1. Contract first, code second

- Write the shapes before the implementation: request/response types, parameter sets, statuses, events, field meaning.
- Record the contract where callers will see it: schema, spec, or exported type with docs, not just in the implementation.
- Name fields for what they are. `userId` is a contract; `data` is not.
- Encode invariants in the shape: required vs optional, units, precision, nullability, allowed values.

## 2. Error semantics are part of the contract

- Every failure mode the caller must react to is a public member: error kinds, status codes, fields.
- Document what is retryable, what is a caller bug, what is a server failure. Retry-ability is a contract decision, not a runtime guess.
- Stable machine-readable error codes; human messages are display strings and may change.
- One envelope across the whole surface (defined in SKILL.md, "Error envelope").

## 3. Validate at the boundary

- Check untrusted input where it enters: the API layer, the event consumer, the CLI parser, not five layers deep.
- Boundary validation produces contract-shaped errors.
- Authn/authz decide identity and access before any business logic runs.
- Internal callers may pass trusted types; do not re-validate every hop and do not skip the boundary.

## 4. Backward compatibility

- Additive by default: new fields, endpoints, statuses, wider accepted input. Never remove, rename, narrow, or reinterpret inside a version.
- Old callers keep working unchanged within the same version. "We control all callers" is not a compatibility story.
- Deprecate with notice and remove only after every caller has migrated.

## 5. Versioning

**One live version at a time.** Compatibility buys a migration window, not a permanent second contract. Two versions are live only during the overlap window of a breaking release, never three. If the repo already runs several versions, follow the repo and do not add another.

Break a contract only when the cost of carrying a wart outweighs the cost of migrating every caller.

Breaking release checklist:

1. Document the diff: what changed, why, the migration path.
2. Deprecation notices: the old surface warns for at least one release; responses carry `Sunset: <date>`.
3. Overlap window: both versions work for one release cycle, then the old one is removed.
4. Migration guide: "replace X with Y, handle Z".
5. Version bump visible to callers: major version, `/v2` path, or new event namespace. Never silent.

Compatible (no bump): new optional response field, new endpoint or status, wider accepted input, new event type in an existing namespace.
Breaking (bump): renamed or removed field, endpoint, status, or event type; narrower input; changed type, semantics, error format, or error codes.

Prefer extending over breaking even when the extension is ugly; a broken caller costs more.

# Plan amendments mid-execution

The plan is Nami's contract; Zoro never edits it directly. When execution
proves the plan wrong (a root cause the plan missed, a task impossible as
written — not a contradiction, which escalates to Luffy), run this loop:

1. **Propose** — to Nami, with evidence (failing command + output) and the
   exact plan diff (task text before → after, no other lines touched).
2. **Approve** — Nami accepts, rejects, or counters. No approval, no change;
   the blocked task waits, other waves continue if disjoint.
3. **Version** — Nami writes the new plan text and appends one row to
   `decisions.md` (what changed, evidence, approver). The old text stays in
   git history — never rewrite, only amend forward.
4. **Continue** — Zoro resumes from the amended task; the amendment row is
   cited in the execution log next to the task's evidence.

Rules: one amendment per proposal (bundled plan rewrites are rejected);
an amendment never widens scope — new scope is a new task via Luffy, not a
silent edit. Emergency (blocked pipeline, fix obvious and tiny): apply,
then file the proposal within the same wave — forgiveness once, never twice.

## The widening test (apply before calling anything an amendment)

"Never widens scope" is felt, not measured, and a felt boundary moves under
pressure. It is an amendment only if ALL THREE hold; any one failing makes it
new scope, which goes to Luffy as a new task:

1. **Files** — every file it touches is already on the task's `Files` line.
   One path not listed there is new scope, however small the edit.
2. **Size** — the task's `Size` class is unchanged. An S that becomes an M is
   a different task wearing the same number.
3. **Acceptance** — the task's acceptance criterion still decides it. If the
   criterion has to be rewritten to cover the change, the change is not what
   the plan approved.

Worked: a task planned as "align one agent's entry block" that turns out to
need the same edit in thirteen agents fails test 1 and test 2. It is a real
finding and the right fix, and it is still a new task — route it, log it,
then do it. Recording it as an amendment is how a 1-file task quietly becomes
a 13-file one with nobody's approval on the difference.

## When the criterion cannot decide

A task whose acceptance turns out to be unverifiable as written (the command
does not exist, the check cannot fail, the criterion was already true before
the task ran) is not "done" and not "blocked" — it is an amendment candidate.
Propose the criterion that would actually decide it, with the evidence that
the written one cannot. Never pass a task on a criterion that could not have
failed.

# Dispatch, batching, resume, phases

Detail behind `mugiwara-execution/SKILL.md`: output rule, worker prompt, report table, batch resume, user tests, and large-campaign layout.

## Task batching and output rule

Run task work tightly: do the steps without narrating each command. Surface one result per task (or per batch): status, evidence link (`[path](relative/path)`), deviations. The checkpoint audits evidence, not commentary. Do not stream every tool call to the main thread. After each task batch, show only:

```
T1: done | built + tested | installer tests pass
T2: done | 7 pointers rewritten | grep for old path: no matches
T3: done | 38/38 tests | full test command
```

Full logs go to `.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/flows/01-execution.md`.

Before dispatching workers, read `heal_cycle`, `heal_halt`, and `repeated_reads` from state: at `heal_halt` stop and escalate; above the repeated-read threshold, skip the re-read or compress it. Details: `_shared/references/cost-governor.md`.

## Worker prompt (parallel workers only)

Sequential work runs inline. Every `[PARALLEL]` worker prompt carries six fields:

- TASK: the task body, verbatim from the plan.
- EXPECTED OUTCOME: what "done" looks like, concrete and checkable.
- REQUIRED TOOLS: commands and files the worker needs.
- MUST DO: the steps in order, including the TDD failing-test-first step.
- MUST NOT DO: files not to touch, configs not to weaken, no silent workarounds.
- CONTEXT: interfaces consumed and produced, related tasks, mission paths.

A prompt shorter than about 30 lines is usually too thin. Thin prompts give thin results.

Workers append their own section (`## <skill> (<task id>)`) to `flows/01-execution.md`. Never overwrite the file.

## Report table

After each stage, show a compact table inline:

```
| # | Task | Status | Evidence |
|---|------|--------|----------|
| T1 | <title> | done / failed | [path](relative/path) |
```

## Batch resume

- Before starting: if `.mugiwara/missions/<mission>/continue.json | continue-<member>.json` exists, resume from its `next_action`. Never re-run completed tasks; verify against the `[x]` marks in `flows/todos.md`.
- After each batch: update `next_action` to the next task.
- A `[PARALLEL]` batch stays inside one sub-mission and never crosses a boundary.
- State proves what is done; continue says what is next (see `mugiwara-orchestration` → `references/resume.md`).

## TDD and user tests

Full TDD: `references/tdd.md`. A test's proof comes from when it runs: a test that passes on its first run proves nothing.

1. User-supplied executable tests are the oracle: run them failing first, green at the end. Never edit or skip them; a change needs the user's consent and a ledger row.
2. A declarative user acceptance criterion becomes a project test file: write it, watch it fail for the intended reason, implement, re-run green. These tests are model-written and can encode the bug, so the checkpoint re-runs them with extra scrutiny.

## Large campaigns (more than 3 phases or a plan over 1500 lines)

- Each phase writes to `flows/phase-NN/`: `01-execution.md`, `02-audit.md`, `03-quality.md`, `04-gates.md`.
- The top-level `flows/` holds only a pointer until archive merges the phases.
- `flows/todos.md` has one `## Phase NN` section per phase.
- Never overwrite a flat `flows/01-execution.md` across phases. Layout of the plan side: `mugiwara-planning`.

# Git Discipline (Zoro, Brook)

## Skip when

- No commits to make in this stage: 0 files staged, nothing to split or amend.
- User handles version control manually for this mission.

Git hygiene keeps the mission reversible: one logical change per commit, a coherent save-point before risky work, and history you can bisect.

## Atomic commits

1. One logical change per commit. A rename, a refactor, and its feature are three commits.
2. Each task commit compiles and passes the relevant checks. Never commit a broken tree.
3. Commit when a unit of work passes its acceptance criteria, not at arbitrary time points.
4. Staging is exact: `git add` specific files and paths, never `git add -A` sweeping an unrelated commit.

## Save-point pattern

A save-point is a local WIP commit on the mission branch, never pushed. It is not a task commit.

1. Before a risky or large operation (refactor, migration, merge), make a save-point only when the tree is in a coherent, runnable state. If it is broken, fix or stash it first; 
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
r vanished.
4. `git log -- <file>` to trace a file's evolution before touching it.

## Never commit secrets

1. Scan before every commit: `.env*`, keys, tokens, passwords, private keys, credentials in code or comments.
2. A secret already committed → treat as compromised: rotate it, purge it from history, file a security finding.
3. Respect `.gitignore`; never force-add an ignored file without a recorded reason.

## Iron Law

EVERY COMMIT IS REVERSIBLE AND EXPLAINABLE. If you cannot name the logical change and why, the commit is not ready.

## Red flags

- A commit mixing refactor and feature, or failing to compile.
- `git add -A` sweeping unrelated files into a commit.
- A save-point skipped before a risky operation, or one made from a broken tree.
- `git reset --hard` run without the user naming what is lost.
- Writing commit messages in a style the repo's history does not use.
- A secret reaching a commit, or a force-added ignored file.

All mean: stop, unstage, and re-stage exactly what belongs together.

# Test-Driven Development

A test proves nothing by existing. It proves nothing by passing. Its entire value lives in WHEN it runs and HOW it fails. TDD is the discipline that makes that proof real.

## Skip when

- No production code written: docs, config, or pure dependency bump.
- Refactor already fully covered by existing passing tests (record the reason).

## When to use

Every task that writes production code — feature, bug fix, refactor, new function. The moment code leaves your keyboard, its test must already have failed first.

## Process

RED:

1. Write exactly one failing test for the next behavior. Name it plainly: `shouldRejectOrderWhenStockIsZero`, not `test2`.
2. Run it. WATCH it fail — for the intended reason (feature missing), not a typo, not a wrong assertion, not a broken harness.
3. A test that fails for the wrong reason proves nothing. If it red-screens on an import error, the proof is that you can't import, not that the feature is missing. Fix the harness, re-watch it fail correctly.
4.

s

- A test that passes without having failed first.
- A red that is a typo, import error, or wrong assertion — you never saw the intended failure.
- Implementation present before its test, "reused as reference".
- One test with a pile of unrelated assertions.
- Mocks verifying internal call sequences instead of outcomes.
- A failing test deleted or weakened to go green.
- A refactor run that never re-runs the suite, or a suite that fails and is refactored anyway.
- An 80/15/5 pyramid that is actually 5/15/80.

All mean: stop, go back to the last green, redo the step honestly.

## Verification

The evidence of a TDD task is the sequence, not the endpoint:

- the red run output (captured), showing the intended failure reason,
- the green run output (captured), after the minimal implementation,
- the refactor pass output, still green,

A report that shows only the final green run is an incomplete report. The checkpoint audits the sequence.

- [ ] Tests query by role/label, never by CSS class or mutable text.
- [ ] Keyboard paths asserted in tests for non-trivial interactions (menu, modal, form submit).

## Performance (Core Web Vitals)

- [ ] Every image has width/height or aspect-ratio — no layout shift on load.
- [ ] LCP asset preloaded; fonts use `font-display: swap`; nothing above the fold lazy-loaded.
- [ ] Below-fold media and routes lazy-loaded; no whole icon/font library imported for a few glyphs.
- [ ] Input handlers free of long tasks; heavy work deferred or chunked (INP).
- [ ] Lighthouse/lighthouse-ci run when the repo has it: performance and accessibility at/above budget, deltas listed.

# Root Cause Process

A failure is a stopping event, not a speed bump. Do not guess, do not patch.
Walk the four phases in order; each gates the next.

## Phase 1 — Reproduce

1. See it fail for the intended reason. Run the failing case as-is, capture the exact error, exit code, and input.
2. No repro = no debugging. If it will not reproduce, record the conditions, mark `unreproducible`, and move on — never fix a ghost.
3. Prove the failure is current: re-run on clean state, not a warm cache or half-applied change.
4. Stop-the-line: a red test or crash halts new work until it is green or escalated.

## Phase 2 — Localize

1. Bisect to the minimal surface. Narrow by time (`git bisect`), by layer (config/test/code/env), or by input (binary search over the failing data).
2. Read the full error before touching anything — line, file, and surrounding code.
3. Grep every caller of the suspect function. A symptom on one path may be a shared root.
4. Ask what changed recently: diff, new deps, config drift.
5. Name the
